rv.q: The King that is left after Hall's humanization project is somehow more real and urgent and whole.

So it's a relief, not to mention a thrill, to report that Katori Hall's "The Mountaintop" -- which arrives with powerful fistfuls of sparky chemistry between Samuel L. Jackson and Angela Bassett -- crackles with theatricality and a humanity more moving than sainthood.
Factor in the double dose of charisma from certifiable stars Samuel L. Jackson and Angela Bassett, and this show has wings.
His final, solemn address to the audience closes the play on a stirring note.
The path to the peak may be uneven, but the view from there is worth it.
Hall steadily gives up every piece of ground she gains, and, for extended stretches, The Mountaintop can feel more like a series of molehills.
Yet it’s hard not to feel that “The Mountaintop” might have worked better in a smaller, lower-profile production.

What undermines “The Mountaintop” is a rather amateurish narrative twist that is apparently so pivotal to the evening’s reason-for-being that the show’s producers have asked reviewers not to reveal it.

Miscasting and directorial overkill turn what could have been a beguiling chamber meditation on fallibility and destiny into an awkward, mawkish blend of docudrama, surreal whimsy and pandering black-history triumphalism.

And then, toward the end, when we feel like we know everything, the playwright digs deeper and The Mountaintop somehow becomes more majestic, inviting each of us in the audience to join the ascent as we see fit.
Katori Hall's "The Mountaintop," which opened Thursday night at the Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre, isn't an easy play to get in step with emotionally.
That it is more spectacle than poetry is one of its shortcomings.
We Live Here” is a melodrama of the “Oh, dear” school: Nearly every sentence made me think, “Oh, dear. I don’t believe a word of this.

Samuel L. Jackson and Angela Bassett bring their considerable star power to bear on Katori Hall's drama about Martin Luther King Jr.'s final night, but the play itself feels more like a missed opportunity than a revelatory theatrical experience.
Still, the actors, and certainly the subject, deserve a higher plane than The Moutaintop provides.
Aside from a stunning coup de theatre in the final 10 minutes, "The Mountaintop" is disappointingly earthbound.
This won the Olivier Award for best new play? The question kept flashing through my mind while sitting through 'The Mountaintop.'

The show's production team has asked reviewers not to reveal any plot twists (i.e., the maid's real identity), but let's just say it's a supernatural revelation that turns what had previously been a mediocre biodrama into a ridiculous embarrassment.
Bassett is even better, stealing the show with her wildly raucous and earthy portrayal that fully mines her character’s humorous and otherworldly qualities.
Frankly, I think the play is well-meaning rubbish that trivializes an extraordinary man.
They are pretty shoddy, preposterous twists, too costly even gratis.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this imagined account of MLK's final night, with Jackson and Bassett's star power praised but Hall's play often deemed thin and broadly executed despite its weighty subject matter.

vs.sum: The Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, though comfort is compromised by tight legroom, especially in the mezzanine. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic architecture and unique murals, but restroom facilities are limited, leading to long lines during intermission.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Copper induction loop available.
